name: Olympus Mons
kicker: Giant shield volcano on Mars · The tallest known volcano in the solar system
dates: Revealed as a volcano by Mariner 9, 1971–72
briefing: Olympus Mons on Mars is the tallest known volcano in the solar system: about 22 kilometers high, roughly two and a half times as tall as Mount Everest stands above sea level. It is about 600 kilometers wide, roughly the size of Arizona, so a person standing near its edge could not even see the summit. It grew so huge because Mars has no moving tectonic plates, so lava kept piling up in the same spot.
answerHtml: Olympus Mons (prompt on Olympus; do not accept “Mount Olympus”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Through telescopes in the 1800s, a bright spot on Mars often looked white, so Giovanni Schiaparelli [“skyah-puh-REL-ee”] named it Nix Olympica, or “the Snows of Olympus.” Spacecraft later revealed that the spot was a giant mountain, often wreathed in clouds.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Martian volcano, the tallest known volcano in the solar system.

tossups.p: When Mariner 9 reached Mars in 1971, a planet-wide dust storm hid nearly the whole surface, and only a few dark spots poked above the dust. One of those spots turned out to be the summit of this mountain.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this huge shield volcano on Mars, named for the home of the Greek gods.

tossups.p: This mountain is ringed by steep cliffs several kilometers tall, and in some places lava flows spilled over those cliffs onto the plains below. Above the cliffs, its slopes rise so gently that it looks more like a giant dome than a steep peak.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this giant Martian volcano, about two and a half times as tall as Mount Everest.

tossups.p: At the top of this mountain sits a cluster of overlapping collapse craters, each formed when an emptied chamber of magma below let the ground cave in. That summit is the highest point on its planet.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this enormous shield volcano in the Tharsis region of Mars, the tallest in the solar system.

tossups.p: Hawaii’s volcanoes form a long chain because the Pacific Plate keeps sliding over a hot spot, but this mountain’s planet has no moving plates, so lava kept piling up in one place for a very long time.
tossups.r: That let this mountain grow far bigger than any volcano on Earth. For 10 points, name this giant volcano on Mars, about 22 kilometers tall.

tossups.p: Weaker gravity, only about 38 percent of Earth’s, let this mountain grow tall without sagging under its own weight. A laser altimeter on the Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft measured its height above Mars’s reference level, the Martian version of sea level.
tossups.r: It rises about 22 kilometers, making it the tallest known volcano in the solar system. For 10 points, name this shield volcano.

tossups.p: This mountain is about 600 kilometers wide, covering an area roughly the size of Arizona. It is so broad that a person standing near its edge could not see its summit, which would be hidden beyond the horizon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this huge shield volcano on Mars, the tallest in the solar system.

tossups.p: Crater counts on its lava flows suggest that some of them erupted only a few million years ago, so this mountain may not be completely extinct. Europe’s Mars Express orbiter took detailed pictures of its summit starting in 2004.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this giant shield volcano on Mars, about 22 kilometers high.

tossups.p: This mountain stands on the northwest edge of the Tharsis region, not far from a row of three other huge volcanoes named Arsia, Pavonis, and Ascraeus [“ass-KREE-us”]. All four are shield volcanoes built by flowing lava.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name the largest of the four, the tallest known volcano in the solar system.

tossups.p: Like Hawaii’s Mauna Loa, this mountain is a shield volcano, built by countless flows of runny basalt lava that spread into a broad, gently sloping dome. Even Mauna Kea, measured from its base on the sea floor, is less than half as tall as this mountain.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Martian volcano, whose name refers to the home of Zeus and the other Greek gods.

tossups.p: Huge lobes of grooved, ridged ground, together called its aureole [“OR-ee-ohl”], spread hundreds of kilometers out from this mountain, possibly left by enormous landslides from its flanks. Scientists still debate exactly how that ground formed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this giant volcano in Mars’s Tharsis region, the tallest volcano in the solar system.

tossups.p: The summit of this mountain, the highest point on its planet, stands about 30 kilometers above the floor of the Hellas impact basin, the lowest point. On Earth, the drop from Mount Everest’s peak to the deepest ocean trench is only about 20 kilometers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this enormous Martian volcano, roughly two and a half times as tall as Mount Everest.

tossups.p: The air at this mountain’s summit has only about one-eighth of the average Martian surface pressure. Clouds of water ice often form around it as winds push air up its slopes, which may explain why it sometimes looked bright through early telescopes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this giant Martian volcano, named for the home of the Greek gods.

tossups.p: In the late 1970s, NASA’s two Viking orbiters photographed this mountain from above in great detail, and their pictures were combined into famous mosaics showing its summit pits and the cliffs around its base.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this shield volcano on Mars, about 600 kilometers wide and 22 kilometers tall.

tossups.p: Venus’s highest peaks, Maxwell Montes, rise about 11 kilometers above that planet’s average surface level, roughly half the height of this mountain. Earth’s tallest mountain above sea level, Mount Everest, reaches less than 9 kilometers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Martian shield volcano, the tallest known volcano in the solar system, about 22 kilometers high.

trap.title: Which giant on Mars?
trap.body: Mars has several record-setting features that are answer lines of their own, like Olympus Mons, the giant canyon Valles Marineris, and the row of three Tharsis volcanoes. Players who hear “Mars” or “Tharsis” may blurt out the planet, and the name tempts others to say Mount Olympus, the Greek mountain where Zeus lived, which is a mythology answer.
trap.fix: “This volcano” or “this mountain,” with record height, Nix Olympica (its old telescope name), the cliffs around its base, or its summit calderas, means Olympus Mons. “This canyon” means Valles Marineris; “this planet” means Mars; Zeus and the Olympian gods mean Mount Olympus. Saying only “Olympus” earns a prompt, so add “Mons.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Olympus Mons (prompt on Olympus; do not accept “Mount Olympus”)
